messages.body_plain:
Hi to all the people again,

I wish to ask you for some opinions-advice in the analysis of some
data. I'm now working on searching and studying snakes in central
Spain, in Mediterranean habitats, and as all of you securily know they
are secretive and difficult to survey, but particularly to obtain
population estimates.
The scarce works I've read uses long-term mark-recapture data to
estimate such parameters, but unfortunately I've not enough funds to
do this long-term research. The fieldwork should be restricted to some
months.

The question is, can I use the abundance induced detectability model
to confidently estimate abundance? It will result in adequate
estimations? At least, could it be used to compare abundances in
different habitats?

My main concern is that the model is based on repeated detection/not
detection data, but when I detect the species it is common that I
found more than one snake. Moreover, in repeated surveys I've found 1,
2 and even 7 snakes in the same places.

Any suggestion or commentary will be welcomed. Many thanks

Pablo

messages.body_plain:
hi Pablo,

 I don't see any reason why you could not apply these methods except perhaps that the underlying distribution of N might not be well approximated by a Poisson distribution and unless you have quite a bit of data estimates can be pretty unstable with a negative binomial model.

 the other issue is that estimates of N from those models do not easily translate into density estimates. That said, if you are surveying areas that are large relative to animal home range size then maybe you could do that in a pretty loose sense.

 The fact that you are obtaining counts of individuals should almost certainly be useful for building more useful models although I gather from your description of the problem that detection of individual snakes is not independent.  That could probably be dealt with somehow.

 Finally, you might try some other methods for surveying snakes such as using distance sampling along transects, using 2 observers to obtain individual encounter history data, or even do some kind of spatial mapping of detections in order to devise territory level encounter histories.

regards
andy

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] abundance induced detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pablo,

You raise many important issues that cannot be fully answered in a short email, but here are a few suggestions. It sounds to me that you are using an "area search" method that would lend itself to quadrat sampling. You could put a grid down over your study area and randomly sample a large number of grid cells (or possibly stratify by habitat type). Let's call these plots. All the abundance models in unmarked assume that each plot has a particular number of snakes associate with it (N_i).  The collection of N_i is assumed to follow some distribution such as the Poisson whose mean can be modeled as a function of habitat variables. If you could perfectly observe N_i, then some sort of generalized linear model would suffice. But since you cannot, you need to estimate the probability of detection. To do that, most models in unmarked require that you collect replicate observations at each plot during a time when the N_i does not change (the population is closed). Suppose that you think the population is closed during a 5 day period. You could survey each plot once/day and then use the N-mixture model of Royle (Biometrics 2004) to estimate total population size and test for differences among habitat types.

The closure assumption can be hard to meet. If this is the case, one option would be to use conduct replicate surveys over a very short time period. Perhaps you could survey each plot 3 times/day, or better yet, use removal sampling. For instance, you could search each plot for 10 minutes or so and put each snake in a bag. Then immediately search it again for 10 minutes and continue to bag snakes. Repeat this several consecutive times. If you do this once per plot, you could use the multinomPois() function in unmarked to estimate population size and model variation in abundance.

However, some of the snakes at your plot will not be available for detection since they hang out underground. So, you could do muliptle removal surveys at each plot. Perhaps once/day for 5 days. Then you could use the "gmultmix" function to estimate both the probability of detection and the probability of being available for detection. We just published a paper about this model. http://www.esajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1890/10-2433.1. The example on the help page shows a similar type of data structure.

Just a suggestion. Hope it helps.

Richard

Hello Pablo-

I thought I would chime in with my comments, but keep in mind I'm a
herpetologist, not a biometrician.

I think you should consider trying to sample in such a way that is
valid to use  make the use of the N-mixture model of Royle (2004).
This sounds to me like an appropriate way for you to sample within
your constraints and get useful abundance data that you can report.

There are some good examples of this model being used in the
literature, and it is available as part of unmarked using the pcount()
model-fitting  function.

Check out Dodd and Dorazio (2004) for a herp example of this model and
also Kery et al. (2005) with birds.  Also, if you are willing to go
Bayesian this model is easily written in WinBUGS.  See Royle et al.
(2007) and Kery and Royle (2010).

Hope this helps.

messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users-

We have fit and selected n-mixture models with habitat covariates at
the plot- and landscape-level for 23 forest passerine species, based
on data from four watersheds.  I now have the luxury (for the first
time!) of an independent data set from a fifth watershed within the
same ecosystem for use in validating our models, but I'm not sure how
to go about it.  I was thinking of using our models and associated
coefficient/beta values for habitat covariates (based on the original
data) to predict spp relative abundance with the values of the habitat
covariates in the validation watershed, and then regressing/
correlating the new predictions with the observed values of spp
relative abundance from the validation watershed.  However, assuming
this is a valid approach, I'm not sure how to handle the detection
error associated with the observed relative abundance data from the
validation watershed.  Perhaps we should "manually" correct the
observed abundance data with the predicted estimates of detection
error from the original models, before regressing the new predictions
with the observed values?  Or maybe you are aware of different
methods?  Most of the literature I have found is focused on using
"resampling" methods (ROC curves, jackknife, cross-validation,
bootstrapping, etc.) to assess model fit without the availability of
an independent data set for validation.

Thanks in advance for your input.  Best regards,

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hi Pablo,

When fitting a removal model with "gmultmix", removals *among* primary sampling periods must be temporary not permanent. For example, you could remove snakes during 3 consecutive 5-minute periods, but then you would need to release them before conducting another round of removals at that plot. Or, if you use only 1 primary period, you do not need to release the snakes, but it will not be possible to estimate the probability of being available for detection.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

I believe what Andy is suggesting is that you compare the observed counts in your "test" watershed (y.test) with the model's predictions (y.hat). Something like this should work:

lam.hat <- predict(yourmodel, newdata=testdata, type="state")[,1]
lam.hat <- matrix(lam.hat, M, J)
p.hat <- predict(yourmodel, newdata=testdata, type="det")[,1]
p.hat <- matrix(p.hat, M, J)

y.hat <- lam.hat * p.hat

So now you just need a measure of predictive error to compare y.hat with y.test (your counts from the new watershed). Something like this might suffice, but you should consult a good text

pred.error <- mean(abs(y.test - y.hat))

You could use this to rank candidate models by their predictive performance (at least the ability to predict data in your new watershed)

Best,
Richard

models for 20 different species and now want to interpret results and

Number of sites=228

#Some of the variables:
dry.site (days into dry season): continuous, range 0-150
water.site (dist to water): continuous, range 0-8000
boma.site(dist to human settlement): continuous, range: 0-10500
use.yr (land use): categorical, "buffer", "ca", "graze", "perm"

umf <- unmarkedMultFrame(bate.history, site.cov.formatted,

with the highest cumulative weight across species) to use for general
comparisons:

single.model <- colext(~scale(dry.site)+scale(water.site)
+scale(boma.site), ~use.yr, ~use.yr, ~occ.obs+year.obs, umf)
